title: Best Affirmation Apps for Depression and Low Mood in 2026
description: The best affirmation apps for depression and low mood in 2026, compared by whether their words are small enough to believe on a flat day, whether the tone is self-compassion rather than demand, whether they can reach you with almost no energy and point at one small action, and what a silent month costs you.
markdown:
By Anicca · November 2026

"Best affirmation app" is the wrong question when what you actually have is not a bad day but a flat one: you wake up already tired, ordinary tasks look oversized, the things that used to interest you have gone quiet, and the voice in your head has settled into a single verdict — you are behind, you are a burden, everyone else is managing and you are not. That state changes what an app has to do, and it changes it more radically than most app pages admit. A person in a low, depressed mood does not need louder positivity. Sentences that claim a wonderful life can land, in that state, as one more piece of evidence that you are failing at feeling. What can help, modestly and honestly, is narrower: words small enough to still be believable, in a tone that is kind rather than demanding, arriving with almost no effort on the days when effort is exactly what is missing — and an app that never turns a silent week into another failure. The apps below are therefore not ranked by who promises the most transformation. They are ranked by what still works, honestly, on the flat days. This comparison follows the same form as our roundups of the best affirmation apps for anxiety, for sleep and racing thoughts at night, for self-esteem and low self-worth, for stress and overwhelm, for overthinking and rumination, for imposter syndrome and the fraud feeling at work, for perfectionism and the flawless-or-failure loop, for social anxiety and the replay after conversations, for burnout and exhaustion that rest does not fix, for a breakup and the urge to check their profile, and for grief after the death of someone you love, re-aimed at depression and persistently low mood.

*Disclosure: Anicca, the app listed sixth here, is made by the team behind this site. It is not ranked first. No app paid to be here. Prices and ratings are from the US App Store listings when we checked on November 19, 2026; check the store page for your country. One boundary before the list itself: depression is a diagnosable, treatable medical condition, and no app on this page — including ours — is a treatment for it. What follows is a comparison of self-help tools for the low days, written for people who are also, where they need it, getting real help.*

## How we judged these, for low mood specifically

1. **Are the words small enough to believe?** This is the first filter, and most affirmation content fails it. In a well-known experiment, people with low self-esteem who repeated the statement "I am a lovable person" ended up in a worse mood than a control group who repeated nothing, while people with high self-esteem felt slightly better (Wood, Perunovic & Lee, 2009). The mechanism matters for every app below: a sentence far from what you currently believe does not lift you toward it; it invites your mind to argue, and the argument wins. Words that stay close to believable — "today I only have to do the next small thing" rather than "I am thriving" — rank above grand claims, and apps that let you shrink a sentence until it is true rank above fixed libraries of big ones.

2. **Is the tone self-compassion, or is it a demand?** Low mood usually arrives with a harsh inner critic already running. A meta-analysis of 14 studies and 4,007 people found that higher self-compassion was associated with lower depression, anxiety and stress, with a correlation of r = −0.54 overall and −0.52 for depression specifically (MacBeth & Gumley, 2012). That is an association, not proof that an app causes anything — but it sets the tone test for this page. Language that speaks to you the way a decent friend would ranks above language that sets a standard ("be your best self", "no excuses") and then measures you against it.

3. **Does it reach you when you have almost no energy, and does it point at a small action?** The evidence-backed treatments for depression are not made of sentences. In a randomised trial of 241 adults with major depression, behavioural activation — a clinician-guided therapy built entirely around scheduling small, valued activities — performed comparably to antidepressant medication among the more severely depressed patients, and significantly better than cognitive therapy in that group (Dimidjian et al., 2006). No app delivers that therapy. But the finding sets a practical test: on a flat day, motivation does not arrive first and action second; it is the other way round. An app that is already on your lock screen, or starts with one press, and whose words can end in one small doable step, is built the right way round. An app that needs setup, streaks and daily check-ins before it gives anything back is built for a person with energy to spare — which is to say, someone else.

4. **What does it cost, and what does a silent month cost you?** Low mood is measured in months, not in a trial week, and a habit study at University College London found a new behaviour took a median of 66 days to feel automatic, with a range of 18 to 254 days (Lally et al., 2010). Judge every app on the long window: what it costs over a year, and whether returning after three silent weeks — a normal feature of a depressive episode, not a lapse of character — feels like resuming or like apologising to a broken streak.

## The six at a glance

| App | Best for | Standout | Get it |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Believe | Writing the small, true sentence yourself, in your own voice | Write your own, voice recording, Soul mirror, categories including health and self-love | iOS · Android |
| Innertune | Sentences that arrive with one press when you cannot start anything | Personalised playlists, 77,000 affirmations, press play and listen hands-free | iOS · Android |
| I am | A different sentence on the lock screen, at scale | 739,660 US ratings, intentions and reminders through the day | iOS · Android |
| Gratitude | A written record of small, real things — evidence, not cheerleading | Private journal with prompts, vision board, write and record your own affirmations | iOS · Android |
| ThinkUp | Your own voice, on a loop, once you have set it up | Record and loop over music, build your own programme | iOS · Android |
| Anicca | One short card, no streak, nothing to fall behind on | Pick a focus — self-love and confidence are among those named — one daily lock-screen line | iPhone |

## 1. Believe: Best for writing the small, true sentence yourself, in your own voice

Believe takes first place here because question 1 is the whole game on this page, and Believe is the only app on this list built around letting you set the size of the claim yourself. You can **write your own affirmations**, **record them in your own voice**, and say them to your own face in the **Soul mirror**. That is how a sentence survives contact with a depressed mind. Not "I am confident and unstoppable", which the argument in your head will dismantle in seconds, but the line that is actually true at your current size: that getting up and making tea counts, that a bad season is a season and not a verdict, that you do not have to feel better today — only to do the next small thing. Its listing organises words by the moment you are in, and the named categories include **self-love** and **health**, alongside confidence before a hard day, calm before sleep, gratitude, mornings, relationships, work, study, money, mindfulness and personal growth, and its current listing adds a free "Mental Health" category. **Timed sessions** with music and calming sounds give one line room to land, and widgets and scheduled reminders cover the timing of question 3. Write the lines on a steadier day, and write them smaller than feels necessary. That written smallness is what the rest of this list is measured against.

Believe launched in June 2021 and showed **4.9 stars from 379 US ratings** when we checked on November 19, 2026. Its US listing shows Believe Premium+ at **$3.99 a month** and a **lifetime option at $69.99** among its in-app purchases.

### Where it falls short

The crowd is elsewhere — 379 ratings against I am's hundreds of thousands. If social proof is your evidence, the evidence is not here. Believe also tracks consistency with practice medals, which cuts directly against question 4: for most people medals are decoration, but if a broken streak would become one more thing you failed at this season, use the sessions and ignore the medals entirely. And the writing, the recording and the mirror all ask something of you up front. On the flattest days, that ask may be more than you have — which is why Innertune, which asks for one press, is second on this page and may be first for you right now.

## 2. Innertune: Best for sentences that arrive with one press when you cannot start anything

Innertune is the app for the days when question 1 cannot even be attempted because starting anything — including an app session — feels like the task itself. Its core practice requires, at the moment of use, exactly one press. Its listing opens with "Stop the negative thought spiral", builds **a personalised playlist for your exact situation** from **77,000 affirmations across 550+ playlists**, and is built to run while you sleep, work or relax. For low mood, that passivity is not a compromise — it is the mechanism, and it matches the logic of question 3: the sentences keep arriving in a channel that does not need your eyes, your hands or your motivation, while you do the one small thing the day allows. Premium lists **19 voices including an ASMR option**, your own-voice recording if you want it later, binaural and sleep beats, a night mode and offline downloads. Its listing names its targets as anxiety and racing thoughts, sleep and restless nights, self-doubt and confidence, and breaking negative thought patterns — the neighbourhood of low mood, even if not its name.

Innertune showed **4.8 stars from 12,149 US ratings** when we checked on November 19, 2026. Its US listing shows premium plans including **$29.99 a year** and **$9.99 a month** among its in-app purchases.

### Where it falls short

A playlist personalised to a situation is still not a sentence sized to your belief — the library's general vocabulary leans toward mindset and momentum, and question 1 warns about exactly that gap: check a playlist's tone on a steadier day before trusting it on a flat one, and skip any track whose claims your mind immediately argues with. Audio playing near you can also fade into the background while the mood continues underneath it, unanswered. And Innertune is a subscription to listening, indefinitely; if what you need is words you eventually own without the app, start with Believe above. Pick Innertune if, right now, "press play" is honestly the size of step available to you. In a low season, that is not a small thing. It is the correct-sized thing.

## 3. I am: Best for a different sentence on the lock screen, at scale

I am is the category default, and its listing starts from a neighbouring observation: "How many negative thoughts have been repeating in your mind?" Its answer is placement and scale. On the App Store since 2014, **4.8 stars from 739,660 US ratings** when we checked on November 19, 2026, it lets you choose daily intentions and set **reminders to be delivered throughout the day**, with widgets and lock-screen lines in a library large enough that the sentence rarely repeats. For low mood, the practical value is a different sentence already on your lock screen in the unplanned moments — the first look at the phone in the morning, the pause before a task you have been avoiding — without opening anything, choosing anything or completing anything. That zero-effort arrival is question 3 done well. Premium is listed at **$59.99 a year** and **$14.99 a month**, with a **lifetime option at $89.99**, on its US store page.

### Where it falls short

The relationship is one-directional. You receive; you rarely make. There is no mirror, no voice recorder and no way to shrink a sentence until it is believable, so the library's size works against question 1 as often as for it: much of the category's general language leans toward achievement, dreams, ambitions and abundance — its listing speaks of verbally affirming your dreams and ambitions and becoming what you believe, and of ensuring every day is an amazing day. For a mind in a depressive episode, that register can read as pressure, and Wood et al. (2009) is the evidence that the pressure is not imaginary. Use I am for interrupting a general loop of self-blame with sheer variety and placement. For words sized to what you can currently believe, it does not compete with the two apps above it.

## 4. Gratitude: Best for a written record of small, real things

Gratitude is built from a private gratitude journal with prompts, a vision board, Daily Zen content, and affirmations you can **listen to or read**, write yourself, set to music and record in your own voice. For low mood, the journal is the active ingredient — used in one specific way, and it is not the way the app's name suggests. Do not use it to force thankfulness; on a flat day, an instruction to count blessings can become another standard to fail. Use it as evidence. Depression edits memory: it keeps the failures and deletes the ordinary completions. A dated line — "walked to the shop", "answered one message", "ate a real lunch" — is a written record, in your own hand, that the day contained what the mood says it did not. That is the closest anything on this page comes to the spirit of question 3: small, real, done things, written down where the edited memory cannot quietly remove them. Its prompts and reminders lower the cost of starting, and the listing stresses that the journal is completely private. It showed **4.9 stars from 44,995 US ratings** when we checked on November 19, 2026, and its US listing shows an annual pro plan at **$29.99** and a monthly plan at **$4.99**. It has been on the App Store since 2018.

### Where it falls short

The frame is gratitude, and the frame is the risk. On the worst days, an app organised around counting good things can feel like an instruction to perform a feeling you do not have, and prompts written for ordinary self-care will sometimes miss the size of what is happening to you entirely. Writing also asks more than listening does: on the days when the flatness is the whole day, the journal will stay closed, and that has to be allowed to cost nothing. And like Believe, its strongest use here — the evidence record — is a use you bring to it, not the use it advertises. If the name of the app itself puts you off in this season, that reaction is information; skip to Innertune or Believe.

## 5. ThinkUp: Best for your own voice, on a loop, once you have set it up

ThinkUp's core idea is the one your brain is built to trust: your own voice. You select affirmations from an expert-approved list or use them as inspiration to **create your own**, **record them in your own voice**, add an image that inspires you, set them to music, and loop the programme with notifications to listen daily. For low mood, the own-voice recording is the real offer, for the same reason Believe ranks first: a sentence you wrote, at a size you chose, said in the voice that lives in your head anyway, has a chance of being believed that a stranger's sentence about success does not. It has been on the App Store since 2014 and showed **4.7 stars from 7,523 US ratings** when we checked on November 19, 2026. Its US listing shows plans including **$7.99 a month**, **$39.99 a year** and a **lifetime option at $99.99** among its in-app purchases.

### Where it falls short

The framing around that recording is achievement language: its listing opens by asking what stops you from achieving goals or becoming who you want to be, and builds toward motivation, prosperity and success. Read against questions 1 and 2, that vocabulary is pointed the wrong way for a depressive episode — you are not a stalled project, and a low season is not a mindset problem. The programme model also assumes setup and daily listening discipline; building the programme is a project, and projects belong on the steadier days, not in the flat ones. Used narrowly — one recorded programme, your words, at believable size, played when you choose — it earns its place. Used as advertised, as a self-improvement system, it will talk past the mood.

## 6. Anicca: One short card, no streak, nothing to fall behind on

Anicca is our app, and it is listed last because on the evidence available today, last is where it belongs on this page. What it does is narrow: you **pick a focus — self-love and confidence are among those named** in its listing — and a new affirmation appears on your **Lock Screen every day**, with short cards you can swipe through at your own pace, save, copy or share, across 8 background themes, in six languages. There is no streak to break, no programme to build, no journal to keep up, and nothing that counts a silent week against you — which, against questions 3 and 4, is the one thing it does exactly right for low mood: it can be left alone for as long as the flat season lasts and resumed without apology. It is iPhone only.

The numbers, stated plainly because this page checks everyone else's: Anicca showed **5.0 stars from 1 US rating** and **4.5 stars from 48 ratings in Japan** when we checked on November 19, 2026. Its US listing shows premium at **$14.99 a month** and **$59.99 a year**. One rating is not social proof of anything, and this page will not dress it up as such.

### Where it falls short

Almost everywhere this page measures. There is no low-mood or depression category, no way to write your own words or record your own voice, and no way to shrink a sentence until it is believable — the exact ability question 1 ranks first. Its named focuses are self-love and confidence, which are neighbouring needs, not this one, and some of its general positive language is larger than a flat day can hold. If your low mood is the thing itself, Believe and Innertune above are built closer to it, and the research section below matters more than any app on this page. Anicca fits a narrower moment: you want one kind line, already on the lock screen, that asks nothing and counts nothing, from an app small enough to be honest about what it is.

## Also worth knowing: Mantra

Mantra, around since February 2017, showed **4.8 stars from 34,492 US ratings** when we checked on November 19, 2026. Its listing opens from the same observation as this page — "Our brains are wired to repeat negative feelings if fed with negative thoughts" — and is built around a daily affirmation you hold with, plus the ability to **read as many affirmations as you like by swiping**, with its library constantly updated. Its US listing shows a monthly plan at **$4.99** and annual plans including **$29.99** among its in-app purchases. It is a credible middle option — a large, established library with a light daily ritual — and the swipe-to-keep-reading form suits the restless, scrolling hour low mood often produces at night. What keeps it off the main list for this page is the same as I am, in smaller form: it is a receiving library, with no route to a sentence sized to your own belief, and its general positive framing needs the steadier-day tone check described under Innertune.

## What the research does — and does not — say

Four findings decide how to use this list, and the first one should be printed on the box of every app on it. First, positive statements can backfire for exactly the people they are sold to. Wood, Perunovic & Lee (2009), in two experiments, had participants repeat the positive self-statement "I am a lovable person" or focus on how it was true. Among participants with **low self-esteem, those who repeated the statement felt worse than those who did not repeat it**; among participants with high self-esteem, the same exercise helped slightly. The authors' conclusion is the rule for this page: repeating positive self-statements may benefit some people, but can backfire for the very people who need them most, because a statement outside what you can currently believe summons the counter-evidence. This is why question 1 outranks library size, voice quality and everything else here — and why, if an app's sentences reliably make you feel worse, the correct response is to stop using those sentences, not to try harder at believing them.

Second, the tone that is associated with lower symptoms is compassion, not demand. MacBeth & Gumley (2012) meta-analysed **14 studies, 20 samples and 4,007 people** and found self-compassion associated with lower psychopathology at **r = −0.54**, with the association for depression at **r = −0.52**. Read it honestly: this is a correlation across mostly observational studies. It does not prove that reading kind sentences lowers depression, and no app on this page can claim it does. What it supports is narrower and still useful — the voice you practise with should sound like the compassionate column of that research, not like a coach shouting at someone who cannot get off the floor.

Third, when depression itself was treated in a trial, what worked was action, guided by a clinician — not affirmations. Dimidjian et al. (2006) randomised **241 adults with major depressive disorder** to behavioural activation, cognitive therapy, antidepressant medication or pill placebo. Among the more severely depressed patients, **behavioural activation was comparable to antidepressant medication, and both significantly outperformed cognitive therapy**. Behavioural activation contains no positive statements at all; it is the scheduled doing of small, valued activities, on the principle that action precedes motivation rather than following it. The lesson for this page is precise and humbling: an app is, at best, a prompt toward that principle — a line on a lock screen that ends in one small step — and it is not a delivery mechanism for the therapy itself. No study cited here tested any app on this page for depression.

The boundary, stated plainly: depression is a medical condition with effective treatments — specific psychotherapies and, where a clinician judges it appropriate, medication — and it is not a failure of positivity, effort or character. Nothing on this page is a treatment for depression or any other condition, including our own app. If your low mood has lasted most of the day, nearly every day, for more than two weeks; if you have lost interest in almost everything, cannot get out of bed, or are not eating or sleeping in a way that is shrinking your life; or if you are having thoughts of harming yourself — that is a conversation for a clinician or a crisis line in your country, today, and it outranks every app above. Asking for that help is not the opposite of self-help. On the evidence, it is the strongest form of it.

The habit research points the same way as in our other comparisons. Lally et al. (2010) found a new behaviour took a median of 66 days to feel automatic, with a range of 18 to 254 days. A counter-practice is still being built in month two — and a depressive episode does not run on that clock anyway — which is why question 4, what it costs over a year and what a silent month costs you, outranks every feature list. A smaller app that costs nothing to resume beats a complete app you stopped opening because resuming it felt like one more thing you had failed to keep up.

## How to choose

- **You want words that are actually believable — written by you, at your size, in your voice:** Believe.
- **You cannot start anything right now and need sentences that arrive with one press, including at night:** Innertune.
- **You want the biggest library and the most social proof, interrupting on your lock screen all day:** I am.
- **Writing small, real, done things down — the evidence record — is how you push back against the edited memory:** Gratitude.
- **Your own voice on a loop is the requirement, and you have a steadier week coming in which to set it up:** ThinkUp.
- **You want one short card, on the focus you chose, with no streak to break and nothing to fall behind on:** Anicca.
